title: Scientific Realism and Its Critics
subtitle: Are electrons real, or just useful? The success of science and the graveyard of theories
objectives: By the end you will be able to define scientific realism by its metaphysical, semantic and epistemic commitments, and contrast it with instrumentalism
By the end you will be able to reconstruct the no-miracles argument and assess the circularity and base-rate objections to it
By the end you will be able to state the pessimistic meta-induction using historical cases such as caloric and the luminiferous aether
By the end you will be able to explain constructive empiricism, structural realism and entity realism as alternative positions
hook:
Nobody has ever seen an electron. Not with the naked eye, not with an optical microscope, not in any ordinary sense of 'see'. Yet physicists describe electrons with extraordinary precision: their charge, their mass, their spin, their behaviour in magnetic fields. The quantum theory of electrons and light predicts one property of the electron (its magnetic moment) to roughly ten significant figures, agreeing with experiment. Our phones, our power grids and our medical scanners are built on these descriptions.

So are electrons real? The question sounds silly until you remember the history of science. Physicists of the nineteenth century were equally confident about **caloric**, a weightless fluid that was supposed to be heat, and about the **luminiferous aether**, an invisible medium filling all space through which light waves were supposed to travel. Both theories made successful predictions. Both entities, we now think, do not exist.

On Day 72 you studied Popper and Kuhn on how science changes. Kuhn's paradigm shifts raised a worry he did not fully resolve: if scientific revolutions overturn the basic picture of the world, why think our current picture is true rather than just the latest fashion? This lesson examines the modern debate over **scientific realism**, one of the central disputes in the philosophy of science. It pits a powerful argument from the success of science against a powerful argument from its history.

sections.heading: What Realists Claim
sections.body:
Following the philosopher **Stathis Psillos** (*Scientific Realism*, 1999), we can separate three commitments of **scientific realism**:

1. **Metaphysical**: there is a world that exists independently of our minds and theories.
2. **Semantic**: scientific theories should be read literally. When a theory says 'electrons have negative charge', it is making a claim that is true or false, and the term 'electron' purports to refer to something real.
3. **Epistemic**: mature, predictively successful theories are **approximately true**, and the unobservable entities they postulate (electrons, genes, black holes) by and large exist.

The main rival view, **instrumentalism**, denies the second or third commitment. Theories are tools, instruments for organising observations and making predictions, not descriptions of a hidden reality. Talk of electrons is useful shorthand, like the lines of longitude on a map: indispensable for navigation, but nobody thinks there are lines painted on the ocean. The logical positivists you met on Day 71 leaned this way, treating theoretical terms as meaningful only through their connection to observations.

History offers a good test case. In the late nineteenth century many respected scientists, including the physicist Ernst Mach and the chemist Wilhelm Ostwald, doubted that atoms were real: they were a handy hypothesis, perhaps, but unobservable and so unscientific to believe in. Then, in work around 1908–1913, the French physicist **Jean Perrin** studied Brownian motion (the jittering of tiny particles in water) and showed that more than a dozen independent methods, from gases, radioactivity, the blue of the sky and Brownian motion itself, all gave approximately the same value for **Avogadro's number**, the number of molecules in a standard quantity of substance. Ostwald conceded that atoms were real. The realist asks: if there were no atoms, why would such different phenomena agree on how many of them there are?

sections.heading: The No-Miracles Argument
sections.body:
That rhetorical question generalises into the most famous argument for realism. **Hilary Putnam** (whom you met in the previous lesson on brains in vats) put it in 1975: realism is the only philosophy that doesn't make the success of science a miracle. The idea had been stated earlier by J. J. C. Smart as a 'cosmic coincidence' argument.

The **no-miracles argument** runs like this:

1. Mature scientific theories are enormously successful, especially at making **novel predictions**: predictions of phenomena nobody had observed or expected, which the theory was not built to accommodate.
2. The best explanation of this success is that the theories are approximately true and their central terms refer to real things.
3. If the theories were false, their success would be an unexplained coincidence, a miracle.
4. Therefore, we should believe that mature, successful theories are approximately true.

A beautiful example of novel prediction: in 1818 Augustin Fresnel submitted a wave theory of light to a competition of the French Academy. The mathematician Siméon Denis Poisson, a sceptic, derived what he thought was an absurd consequence: if Fresnel was right, a bright spot should appear at the very centre of the shadow of a small circular disc. François Arago performed the experiment and found the spot. Fresnel won the prize.

The argument is an **inference to the best explanation** (IBE): we accept a hypothesis because it best explains the evidence. Detectives, doctors and scientists all reason this way.

Critics raise two main objections. First, **circularity**: realists use IBE to argue that scientific theories (which are themselves accepted by IBE) are true. But whether IBE leads to truth is precisely what an anti-realist doubts. Arthur Fine and Larry Laudan pressed this point. Realists reply that the circularity is 'rule-circular' rather than vicious, like using memory to check that memory is generally reliable.

Second, **Bas van Fraassen** offered a rival, Darwinian explanation of success. Theories are successful because unsuccessful ones are weeded out, as mice that fail to flee cats are eliminated. You don't need to suppose that the surviving mice understand cats, only that they survived a selection process. Likewise, surviving theories needn't be true; they are simply the ones that passed the tests so far. Realists respond that selection explains why we *have* successful theories but not why a *particular* theory goes on making novel predictions in new domains.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Does the No-Miracles Argument Ignore the Base Rate?
sections.body:
A newer objection, pressed by Colin Howson (2000) and by P. D. Magnus and Craig Callender (2004), uses exactly the Bayesian tools of the previous lesson. The no-miracles argument says: if a theory were false, success would be very unlikely; so a successful theory is probably true. But that is reasoning from P(success | false) to P(false | success), the move that tripped up the doctors in Eddy's study.

Let us put in numbers. Suppose:

- P(success | approximately true) = 1. True theories reliably succeed.
- P(success | false) = 0.05. Only 1 in 20 false theories would succeed this well by luck. This is what makes success seem 'miraculous' for a false theory.

Now we need a **base rate**: among all the candidate theories that scientists might come up with in a field, what fraction are approximately true? Suppose it is 1%. Then:

> P(true | success) = (1 × 0.01) ÷ (1 × 0.01 + 0.05 × 0.99) = 0.01 ÷ 0.0595 ≈ 0.17

Only about 17%. Despite the 'miracle' intuition, most successful theories would be false, simply because false theories vastly outnumber true ones. If instead the base rate were 50%, the same calculation gives about 95%.

The moral: the no-miracles argument, taken alone, cannot establish realism. It needs an estimate of the base rate of truth among candidate theories, and we have no independent way to measure it, since we only learn which theories were true via the very successes in question. Realists answer that we can look at the *track record*: but that leads straight into the next argument, which says the track record is dismal.

sections.heading: The Pessimistic Meta-Induction
sections.body:
In 1981 **Larry Laudan** published 'A Confutation of Convergent Realism', which turned the history of science against realism. He listed theories that were once empirically successful but whose central terms, by our current lights, refer to nothing. His list included:

- The crystalline spheres of ancient and medieval astronomy.
- The humoral theory of medicine (recall Hippocrates and Galen).
- **Phlogiston** theory, which explained burning as the release of a substance called phlogiston, before Lavoisier's oxygen.
- The **caloric** theory of heat, which explained a great deal of thermodynamics, including the work of Sadi Carnot on steam engines.
- The **luminiferous aether**, the medium of light waves in Fresnel's and Maxwell's physics.
- Theories of spontaneous generation and vital force.

The argument is a **meta-induction**, an induction about scientific theories themselves, sometimes called the **pessimistic meta-induction**. Most past successful theories turned out false. Our current theories are in the same position as theirs were. So, probably, our current theories will also turn out false. Fresnel's spot shows how painful this is: his wave theory made a stunning novel prediction, yet it described light as vibrations of an elastic aether that does not exist. Success, even novel success, does not guarantee reference.

**Kyle Stanford** (*Exceeding Our Grasp*, 2006) added the **problem of unconceived alternatives**. Historically, scientists repeatedly failed to conceive of rival theories that were equally well supported by the evidence available to them, which were later discovered and accepted. Darwin's contemporaries didn't conceive of Mendelian genetics. If this pattern continues, we should expect that our best theories also have unconceived rivals, so we cannot confidently infer their truth by eliminating the alternatives we know about.

Realists have replied in several ways. Some argue the list is cherry-picked: many past theories (the heliocentric solar system, the circulation of the blood, the existence of cells) survived. Others argue that science today is vastly larger, more precise and more interconnected than in the past, so the induction from the past is weak. The most influential reply, however, accepts that something was wrong with past theories, and asks *what survived*.

sections.heading: Selective and Structural Realism
sections.body:
Look closely at Fresnel. His theory said light was a vibration in an elastic aether. That part was abandoned. But his **equations**, which describe how much light is reflected and refracted at a boundary, were carried over almost unchanged into Maxwell's electromagnetic theory, where light is a wave in the electromagnetic field. Fresnel was wrong about *what* was vibrating but right about the mathematical *structure* of how light behaves.

In a 1989 paper, 'Structural Realism: The Best of Both Worlds?', **John Worrall** turned this into a position. **Epistemic structural realism** says: we should believe what our best theories say about the **structure** of the unobservable world, the relations captured in their mathematics, but remain agnostic about the **nature** of the things that stand in those relations. This explains the no-miracles intuition (theories succeed because they capture real structure) while accommodating the pessimistic meta-induction (the stuff posited behind the structure keeps changing).

A more radical version, **ontic structural realism**, defended by James Ladyman and Don Ross in *Every Thing Must Go* (2007), says structure is all there is: at the fundamental level, quantum physics suggests there are no individual 'things' with intrinsic natures, only relations. (Compare Nagarjuna's emptiness in the World track: nothing has svabhava, intrinsic nature.)

A broader family of views, **selective realism** (Philip Kitcher, Stathis Psillos), says we should believe in the parts of theories that actually did the work in producing successful predictions. Caloric theory's successes, Psillos argued, flowed from laws about heat flow that survived, not from the hypothesis that heat was a material fluid.

Critics ask whether we can identify the 'working parts' *in advance*, or only with hindsight after the theory has been replaced. If only with hindsight, selective realism gives us no guidance about which parts of current theories to believe. And structural realists face a technical worry, known since the mathematician M. H. A. Newman's 1928 critique of Russell: if 'structure' is described too abstractly, almost any collection of things of the right size can be arranged to have it, so knowing only structure is to know almost nothing.

sections.heading: Van Fraassen's Constructive Empiricism and Hacking's Entity Realism
sections.body:
The most influential modern anti-realist is **Bas van Fraassen**, whose book *The Scientific Image* (1980) revived the debate. He calls his position **constructive empiricism**. In his formulation, science aims to give us theories that are **empirically adequate**, and accepting a theory involves believing only that it is empirically adequate. A theory is empirically adequate if what it says about **observable** things and events is true. About unobservables, the constructive empiricist suspends judgement. She can use electron theory fluently, build machines with it and teach it, while remaining agnostic about whether electrons exist.

Crucially, van Fraassen does not say theories are mere instruments or that talk of electrons is meaningless; he accepts the realist's semantic thesis. His disagreement is purely **epistemic**: belief should go no further than the evidence of observation can reach.

What counts as observable? For van Fraassen, something is observable if beings like us could perceive it with unaided senses under suitable circumstances. The moons of Jupiter are observable (astronauts could fly close and look); a single electron is not. The obvious objection, made earlier by Grover Maxwell (1962), is that there is a **continuum**: looking through a window, through spectacles, a magnifying glass, a light microscope, an electron microscope. Where is the line, and why should it matter so much? Van Fraassen replies that 'observable' is vague, like 'bald', but vagueness does not erase the difference between clear cases.

The Canadian philosopher **Ian Hacking**, in *Representing and Intervening* (1983), took a different route to realism. He shifted attention from *theories* to *experimental practice*. Physicists at Stanford, he recounted, sprayed positrons and electrons onto a niobium ball to change its charge. His famous verdict: so far as he was concerned, if you can spray them, then they are real. This is **entity realism**: we are entitled to believe in entities we can reliably manipulate to investigate other things, even if our theories about them are incomplete or wrong. You can be confident electrons exist while doubting much of what any particular theory says about them.

No position has won. Arthur Fine's **natural ontological attitude** (1984) suggests we stop asking the question in its philosophical form and simply accept science's results as we accept ordinary truths, without adding either a realist or an anti-realist gloss.

keyQuote.text: The positive argument for realism is that it is the only philosophy that doesn't make the success of science a miracle.
keyQuote.source: Hilary Putnam, Mathematics, Matter and Method (1975)

modernConnection.title: Dark Matter, the Higgs Boson and Black-Box AI
modernConnection.body:
The realism debate is live in today's science. In 2012, physicists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider announced the discovery of a particle consistent with the **Higgs boson**, predicted in 1964. No one 'saw' it; it was inferred from the statistical pattern of decay products in vast numbers of collisions. A realist sees a triumph of novel prediction. A constructive empiricist sees a confirmed prediction about detector readings, and suspends judgement on the particle itself. Hacking might ask whether we can yet *use* Higgs bosons to intervene on anything else.

**Dark matter** is a sharper case. Astronomers infer it from galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing and the cosmic microwave background, and it is estimated to make up around 85% of the matter in the universe. Yet decades of direct-detection experiments have found no dark matter particle. Some physicists defend alternatives that modify the laws of gravity instead (such as MOND). This looks very like the situation of the aether: a successful posit whose nature remains elusive. Structural realism suggests we can be confident about the gravitational structure without knowing what the stuff is.

Machine learning poses the question in a new form. Deep learning systems such as DeepMind's AlphaFold (2020) predict protein structures with remarkable accuracy, but the networks do not offer a humanly interpretable theory of why proteins fold as they do. Some commentators have suggested science may become increasingly instrumentalist: prediction without explanation. Realists reply that such models are tools within a larger realist science that still aims at understanding.

The comparison with the historical debate is apt but imperfect. An AI model is not a theory that posits unobservable entities; it may posit nothing at all. It forces us to ask whether science's aim is truth, empirical adequacy, or simply control, and whether those can come apart. Van Fraassen would say they already do, every day.

vocabulary.definition: The view that mature, successful scientific theories are approximately true and that the unobservable entities they posit by and large exist.
vocabulary.example: A scientific realist believes electrons exist, not just that electron theory makes good predictions.

vocabulary.definition: The view that scientific theories are tools for prediction and organisation of observations, not literal descriptions of unobservable reality.
vocabulary.example: Mach's instrumentalism treated atoms as a useful fiction.

vocabulary.definition: The argument that the predictive success of science would be a miracle unless its theories were approximately true.
vocabulary.example: The no-miracles argument points to the Poisson spot as success too striking to be luck.

vocabulary.definition: Accepting a hypothesis because it would, if true, best explain the available evidence.
vocabulary.example: A detective uses inference to the best explanation when the muddy footprints point to the gardener.

vocabulary.definition: The argument that since most past successful theories turned out false, our current successful theories probably will too.
vocabulary.example: Laudan's list of caloric, phlogiston and the aether fuels the pessimistic meta-induction.

vocabulary.definition: The view that we should believe what successful theories say about the mathematical structure of the world, not about the nature of the entities behind it.
vocabulary.example: Structural realism notes that Fresnel's equations survived although his aether did not.

vocabulary.definition: Van Fraassen's view that science aims at empirical adequacy, and accepting a theory requires believing only what it says about observables.
vocabulary.example: A constructive empiricist can use quantum mechanics daily while suspending judgement on electrons.

vocabulary.definition: Hacking's view that we should believe in unobservable entities we can reliably manipulate, even if our theories about them may be false.
vocabulary.example: Entity realism says spraying electrons onto a niobium ball shows electrons are real.

thinkingExercise.title: Placing Your Bets on Today's Science
thinkingExercise.prompt: Take the realism debate out of the past and apply it to current science.
steps: List three entities posited by current science that you have never observed (for example: genes, black holes, dark matter, quarks, the Higgs boson).
For each, rate your confidence (0–100%) that it exists. Then ask: is your confidence based on predictive success, on our ability to manipulate it, or on authority?
Apply the pessimistic meta-induction: for which of the three can you imagine a future scientist saying 'that was our generation's aether'? What would they keep?

Decide which position (full realism, structural realism, entity realism, constructive empiricism) best matches your ratings, and write a paragraph defending it against its strongest objection from this lesson.

summary: Scientific realism combines metaphysical, semantic and epistemic commitments; instrumentalism treats theories as tools, and Perrin's work on atoms shows the debate's stakes.
The no-miracles argument infers approximate truth as the best explanation of success, especially novel prediction like the Poisson spot.
Critics charge circularity, offer van Fraassen's Darwinian explanation of success, and show with Bayesian numbers that the argument needs an unknown base rate.
Laudan's pessimistic meta-induction lists successful but false past theories (caloric, aether); Stanford adds the problem of unconceived alternatives.
Structural and selective realists argue that mathematical structure and 'working' posits survive theory change, though identifying them in advance is hard.
Van Fraassen's constructive empiricism limits belief to empirical adequacy; Hacking's entity realism grounds belief in our ability to manipulate entities.

quiz.question: Which commitment does van Fraassen's constructive empiricism reject?
options: The metaphysical claim that a mind-independent world exists
The semantic claim that theories should be read literally
The epistemic claim that we should believe successful theories' claims about unobservables
The claim that science makes predictions
quiz.explanation: Van Fraassen accepts literal reading but says acceptance requires believing only in empirical adequacy, suspending judgement about unobservables.

quiz.question: Why was the Poisson bright spot such powerful evidence for Fresnel's theory?
options: It was a novel prediction that seemed absurd and was then confirmed
It was observed with an electron microscope
quiz.explanation: Poisson derived the spot as an objection; Arago's observation made it a striking novel prediction.

quiz.question: Van Fraassen explains the success of science by saying theories are selected for success, like organisms in Darwinian evolution.
quiz.explanation: Unsuccessful theories are eliminated, so surviving ones are successful without needing to be true.

quiz.question: In the lesson's worked example, if P(success | true) = 1, P(success | false) = 0.05 and only 1% of candidate theories are true, what is P(true | success)?
quiz.explanation: 0.01 ÷ (0.01 + 0.0495) ≈ 0.17; ignoring the base rate overstates the case for realism.

quiz.question: The pessimistic meta-induction is an induction over:
quiz.explanation: It reasons from the fate of past successful theories to the probable fate of current ones.

quiz.question: What does Worrall's structural realism say survived the transition from Fresnel's theory to Maxwell's?
options: The idea that light is a particle
The mathematical equations describing reflection and refraction
quiz.explanation: Fresnel's equations carried over even though the nature of what vibrates changed.

quiz.question: Kyle Stanford's problem of unconceived alternatives argues that scientists have historically failed to imagine well-supported rival theories that were later accepted.
quiz.explanation: Stanford uses this historical pattern to argue we should expect unconceived rivals to our current theories.

quiz.question: A lab routinely uses beams of neutrons to probe the structure of materials, though theories of the neutron's internal structure keep changing. Which position most directly supports believing neutrons are real?
quiz.explanation: Entity realism grounds belief in reliable manipulation of an entity to investigate other things, regardless of theory change.

quiz.question: Grover Maxwell's continuum argument challenges van Fraassen by claiming that:
options: Observation shades gradually from naked eye to microscopes, so the observable/unobservable line is arbitrary
Inference to the best explanation is circular
quiz.explanation: The gradual series of instruments suggests no principled line; van Fraassen replies that vague distinctions can still be real.

quiz.question: The realist's reply to the circularity objection is that using IBE to defend IBE is rule-circular, like using memory to check memory.
quiz.explanation: Realists argue rule-circularity is not vicious, though anti-realists remain unconvinced.

goDeeper.body:
The realism debate has become more fine-grained in recent decades. One line examines specific historical cases in depth. Hasok Chang's studies of phlogiston (*Is Water H2O?*, 2012) argue provocatively that phlogiston theory was abandoned too quickly and captured real chemical relations (roughly, what we would call electrons and chemical potential), complicating the standard story used both by realists and by Laudan. Peter Vickers and others have examined whether 'idle' posits, the parts of false theories that did no predictive work, can really be identified, as selective realists require.

A second line concerns the **base-rate fallacy** objection. Some realists, like Psillos, reply that the no-miracles argument was never a probabilistic argument about a population of theories but an explanatory argument about each particular theory. Others try to estimate the base rate from scientific practice: scientists don't generate random theories but constrain them heavily by background knowledge, so the proportion of true candidates may be far higher than 1%.

A third line, **perspectival realism** (Ronald Giere, Michela Massimi), holds that scientific knowledge is always from a historically and culturally situated perspective, yet can still be knowledge of a real world. Massimi's *Perspectival Realism* (2022) argues that multiple perspectives, each limited, can jointly track real phenomena.

Finally, quantum mechanics poses a special challenge: different interpretations (Copenhagen, many-worlds, Bohmian mechanics, collapse theories) are empirically equivalent so far but describe radically different realities. If realists cannot say which is true, what exactly are they being realist about? This is underdetermination in its starkest current form.

questions: Is the pessimistic meta-induction itself vulnerable to a meta-meta-induction: past philosophical arguments about science have mostly been wrong, so this one probably is too?
If a predictive AI system outperforms all human theories but offers no explanation, has science achieved its aim?
Does Hacking's criterion ('if you can spray them') make the reality of entities depend on our technology? Is that a problem?
